text: a million evaluations to price an option on 100 stocks, an average over 100 inputs, and even grid feels thorough. How many values does each input get? One, the whole grid is one point, the center of the box. Two values per input would take two to the hundredth points. Since Metropolis and Ulam's 1949 paper, the standard tool has been random points, like this one. how far off would a million of them land? Start with two inputs, a square. Our function is one inside this quarter disk, zero outside, so its average is the disk share. Exactly one half. A 10 by 10 grid puts 52 of its 100 points inside, two points off. 100 random darts put 44 inside, six points off. In two dimensions, the grid wins. Now give each a million points and add inputs. The disc becomes a ball grown just enough to cover exactly half the box. The grid splits its million across the axes. A thousand values per axis in two dimensions, then a hundred, ten, three. From 20 dimensions on, just the center, which sits inside the ball. So the grid says the ball fills the box, 50 points off. Even two values on 19 axes, half a million points, is 18 points off. The darts stay under a tenth of a point. Look at the shadows on one axis. The grid's 100 points cast 10, 100 darts cast 100, with n points over d axes. Each axis gets the dth root of n. But shadows alone are not the fix. A million points on the diagonal, each one a flat line here, give every axis a million values and still miss by 8 points. Their coordinates move in lockstep A dart coordinates are drawn independently so it lands inside with a chance equal to the answer in two dimensions or a hundred Their estimate is a share of heads in n-coin flips. One flip is zero or one. Its average is a half, and every flip misses that by exactly a half. Repeat the 100 dart experiment 300 times. In two dimensions or a hundred, the estimates spread this wide. Quadruple the darts, and both get twice as narrow. Each dart misses by a half, up or down at random, so the misses partly cancel. 16 darts stray about 4 halves, not 16. N darts stray about root N halves. Divide by the N darts. A half over root N. With 100 darts, that's 5 points. We measured 4.8. Any other function swaps that half for its own spread, sigma. The root N remains, and there's no D in it. A grid's miss, even for smooth functions, has d in its exponent. The exponents tie at four dimensions, near where our lines crossed. So, back to our ball, with a million darts in any dimension. How far off is a typical estimate? One-half over a thousand, five-hundredths of a point. In 2012, Bergstra and Bengio found that random search tuned neural networks as well as grid search, in a fraction of the time. If one setting matters most, nine grid trials test three values of it, nine random trials test nine. Darts do have a blind spot, tiny answers, fix the radius at one, and by 30 dimensions the ball fills two parts in a hundred trillion of the box. Below this line, a million darts expect under one hit, so they usually report zero. Off by the whole answer. The darts never notice the axes. A million coin flips, in any dimension.
